summary: Defines an IMAP extension that lets a client ask for specific unsolicited notifications about chosen mailboxes, such as messages being added or deleted. This is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5267.

plainLanguage.summary: A mail client usually has to keep asking the server whether anything has changed. This RFC lets the client register once for the kinds of change it cares about, on the folders it cares about, and the server then tells it as they happen.

questions: how to get push notifications from imap
how to watch multiple mailboxes in imap
subtitle: An IMAP command that lets a client register for the mailstore events it wants the server to push.

tldr.problem: IMAP clients had no way to say which changes they wanted to hear about. The IDLE command pushed everything about the selected mailbox only, and needed a connection per mailbox.
tldr.mechanism: A new NOTIFY command registers a set of mailboxes and event types. The server then pushes untagged responses for those events, and the client can ask for message attributes with each one.
tldr.outcome: A client can watch several folders on one connection and receive only the events it asked for. The server can refuse a request that would be too expensive, and can switch notifications off if a client floods it.

today: RFC 5465 is a Proposed Standard from February 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. NOTIFY was added to the list of IMAP extensions, and the OLDNAME extended data item was registered with the LIST-EXTENDED registry from RFC 5258.

sections.title: Why a Client Needs to Say What It Wants to Hear
sections.content:
The IDLE command provides a way for the client to go into a mode where the IMAP server pushes it notifications about IMAP mailstore events for the selected mailbox. However, the IDLE extension does not restrict or control which server events can be sent, or what information the server sends in response to each event. Also, IDLE only applies to the selected mailbox, thus requiring an additional TCP connection per mailbox.

This document defines an IMAP extension that allows clients to express their preferences about unsolicited events generated by the server. The extension allows clients to only receive events that they are interested in, while servers know that they do not need to go to the effort of generating certain types of untagged responses.

Without the NOTIFY command, an IMAP server will only send information about mailstore changes to the client as the result of a client command, as unsolicited responses sent just before the end of a command, or during an IDLE command. The NOTIFY command extends what information may be returned in those last two cases, and also permits and requires the server to send information about updates between commands. It also allows the client to extend what information is sent unsolicited about the selected mailbox and to request some update information to be sent regarding other mailboxes.

For new messages delivered to or appended to the selected mailbox, the NOTIFY command can be used to request that a set of attributes be sent to the client in an unsolicited FETCH response. This allows a client to be a passive recipient of events and new mail and to maintain full synchronisation without having to issue any subsequent commands except to modify the state of the mailbox on the server.
sections.plainLanguage: IDLE makes the server tell the client everything about one mailbox. That is too much and too narrow at the same time. NOTIFY lets the client list the folders and the changes it wants, and ask for extra detail with each change, so one connection can cover several folders.

sections.title: The NOTIFY Command
sections.content:
IMAP servers that support this extension advertise the NOTIFY capability. The NOTIFY command informs the server that the client listens for event notifications all the time, even when no command is in progress, and requests the server to notify it about the specified set of events. It has two forms. NOTIFY NONE specifies that the client is not interested in any kind of event happening on the server. NOTIFY SET replaces the current list of interesting events with a new list.

Until the NOTIFY command is used for the first time, the server only sends notifications while a command is being processed, and notifies the client about MessageNew, MessageExpunge or FlagChange events on the selected mailbox. The effect of a successful NOTIFY command lasts until the next NOTIFY command or until the IMAP connection is closed. A successful NOTIFY SET command must cause the server to immediately return any accumulated changes to the currently selected mailbox, so a successful NOTIFY SET implies an implicit NOOP command.

If the NOTIFY command enables MessageNew, MessageExpunge, AnnotationChange or FlagChange notifications for a mailbox other than the currently selected mailbox, and the client has specified the STATUS indicator parameter, then the server must send a STATUS response for that mailbox before NOTIFY's tagged OK. If MessageNew is enabled the STATUS response must contain MESSAGES, UIDNEXT and UIDVALIDITY; if MessageExpunge is enabled it must contain MESSAGES; and if AnnotationChange or FlagChange are included and the server also supports CONDSTORE or QRESYNC, it must contain UIDVALIDITY and HIGHESTMODSEQ.

For each mailbox specified, the server verifies that the client has access. If the name does not refer to an existing mailbox, the server must ignore it. If the name refers to a mailbox that the client cannot list, the server must ignore it, which prevents disclosure of potentially confidential information. If the client can list the mailbox but lacks another right needed for the specified events, the server must respond with an untagged extended LIST response containing the NoAccess name attribute. The server should return the tagged OK response if the client has access to at least one of the mailboxes in the current list.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends NOTIFY SET with the folders and the events it wants. The server checks that the client is allowed to see each folder, ignores the ones it is not, and answers OK. The setting lasts until the client changes it or the connection ends.

sections.title: The Event Types
sections.content:
Only some of the events in the mailstore event specification can be expressed in IMAP, and for some of them there are several possible ways to express the event. The server should omit notifying the client if the event is caused by that client, for example a CREATE command that creates a mailbox the client asked to be told about. All event types require the lookup and read rights on all observed mailboxes.

If the FlagChange or AnnotationChange events are specified, MessageNew and MessageExpunge must also be specified. If one of MessageNew or MessageExpunge is specified, then both must be specified. Otherwise the server must respond with the tagged BAD response. The client can instruct the server not to send an event by omitting it, by using the NONE event specifier, or by using NOTIFY NONE.

For a flag or annotation change in the selected mailbox, the server notifies the client by sending an unsolicited FETCH response that must include UID and FLAGS or ANNOTATION fetch data items. For a change in another mailbox, the server responds with a STATUS response. For a new or appended message in the selected mailbox, the server sends an unsolicited EXISTS response followed by an unsolicited FETCH response containing the information the client requested. For a new message in another mailbox, the server sends an unsolicited STATUS response with UIDNEXT and MESSAGES. An expunged message in the selected mailbox is reported with EXPUNGE, or VANISHED where the QRESYNC extension is in use, and in another mailbox with a STATUS response.

A mailbox that was created, deleted or renamed produces an unsolicited LIST response for the affected name, and a renamed mailbox produces an extended LIST response carrying the OLDNAME extended data item with the old name. A subscription change produces an unsolicited LIST response including the Subscribed attribute when, and only when, the mailbox is subscribed after the event. Mailbox and server metadata changes produce unsolicited METADATA responses.
sections.plainLanguage: There are eight kinds of event. New mail, deleted mail and flag changes arrive as FETCH responses for the open folder and as STATUS responses for other folders. Folder creation, deletion and renaming arrive as LIST responses. The client chooses which of them it wants.

sections.title: Which Mailboxes to Watch
sections.content:
Mailboxes to be monitored can be specified in several different ways. Only SELECTED and SELECTED-DELAYED match the currently selected mailbox; all other mailbox specifications affect other mailboxes. Multiple event groups can apply to the same mailbox, so a client can ask for message events on a folder from one group and a subscription event on it from another.

Only one of the two specifiers affecting the currently selected mailbox can be specified in any NOTIFY command. Both refer to the mailbox that was selected using SELECT or EXAMINE, and when the connection is not in the selected state they refer to no mailbox. The two specifiers apply only to message events, and it is an error to specify other types of events with either of them.

The SELECTED specifier requires the server to send immediate notifications for the currently selected mailbox about all specified message events. The SELECTED-DELAYED specifier requires the server to delay a MessageExpunge event until the client issues a command that allows returning information about expunged messages, for example a NOOP or an IDLE command, and the server may also delay other message events or return them immediately.

The other specifiers are personal, which refers to all selectable mailboxes in the user's personal namespaces; inboxes, which refers to the personal mailboxes that a delivery agent may deliver messages to, and which the server must treat as equivalent to personal if it cannot easily compute the set; subscribed, which refers to all mailboxes the user is subscribed to; subtree, which is followed by a mailbox name or list of names and refers to all selectable mailboxes subordinate to them plus the named mailboxes themselves; and mailboxes, which is followed by a name or list of names and where the server must not do a wildcard expansion.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can name folders one by one, ask for everything below a folder, ask for everything it is subscribed to, or ask for the open folder only. For the open folder there are two settings: notify at once, or hold back deletion notices until the client next asks.

sections.title: How NOTIFY and IDLE Work Together
sections.content:
If IDLE, as well as this extension, is supported, then while processing any IDLE command, the server must send exactly the same events as instructed by the client using the NOTIFY command.

NOTIFY makes IDLE unnecessary for some clients. If a client does not use message sequence numbers and the wildcard in commands, it can request MessageExpunge and MessageNew for the selected mailbox by using the NOTIFY command instead of entering the IDLE mode. A client that does use message sequence numbers and the wildcard can still use the NOTIFY command if it specifies the SELECTED-DELAYED mailbox specifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The two commands do not conflict. While the client is in IDLE, it gets the same events it registered for, and a client that does not rely on message numbers can skip IDLE altogether and just use NOTIFY.

sections.title: Extending SEARCH and SORT
sections.content:
If the server that supports the NOTIFY extension also supports CONTEXT=SEARCH or CONTEXT=SORT, the UPDATE return option is extended so that a client can request that FETCH attributes be returned when a new message is added to the context result set.

The EXISTS response must precede any FETCH responses, and together they must precede the ESEARCH response. No untagged FETCH response should be returned if a message becomes a member of an UPDATE search because of flag or annotation changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A client that searches for mail can also be told when a new message matches the search, and can ask for the same message details as with any other new mail.

sections.title: The Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax is given in Augmented Backus-Naur Form, with the non-terminals capability, command-auth, mailbox, mailbox-data, resp-text-code and search-key defined in the IMAP4 specification, the modifier-update non-terminal defined in the CONDSTORE and SEARCH extension, and mbx-list-oflag defined in the IMAP4 specification and updated by the LIST-EXTENDED extension. All alphabetic characters are case-insensitive, and implementations must accept these strings in a case-insensitive fashion.

The grammar adds NOTIFY to the capability list and to the authenticated commands. The notify production takes either a notify-set, which is the word SET, an optional status indicator and a list of event groups, or a notify-none, which is the word NONE. Each event group is a mailbox filter followed by a list of events, and each event is a message event, a mailbox event, a user event or an extension event.
sections.plainLanguage: The grammar records that the command is SET with groups of folders and events, or NONE, and that a client may name an event type it does not recognise so that later extensions can add more.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
It is very easy for a client to deny itself service using NOTIFY. Asking for all events on all mailboxes may work on a small server, but with a big server can swamp the client's network connection or processing capability. In the worst case, the server's processing could also degrade the service it offers to other clients.

Server authors should be aware that if a client issues requests and does not listen to the resulting responses, the TCP window can easily fill up, and a careless server might block. This problem also exists in plain IMAP, however this extension magnifies the problem.

This extension makes it possible to retrieve messages immediately when they are added to the mailbox. This makes it wholly impractical to delete sensitive messages using programs like imapfilter. Using SIEVE or similar is much better.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking for too much can hurt the client as much as the server, and a client that asks and then stops reading can block the server. The RFC also warns that mail-filtering programs that delete messages will not work if the client receives messages the instant they arrive, so server-side filtering is the better tool.
